claims.text: Applying a strong static magnetic field during solidification can increase the coercive field of magnetic high-entropy alloys relative to solidification without the field.
The intervention is applicable to an as-cast alloy state.
The intervention is applicable to an annealed alloy state.
The effect should hold at room temperature.
The effect should hold at standard atmospheric pressure.
A strong static magnetic field applied during solidification alters microstructure evolution.
A strong static magnetic field applied during solidification alters phase separation or phase constitution.
Changes in microstructure and phase constitution mediate changes in coercivity.
The microstructural and phase changes caused by the field produce an increase in coercive field.
The alloy has a low coercive field when solidified without a strong static magnetic field.
The coercivity response to a strong static magnetic field may depend on alloy composition.
The coercivity response to a strong static magnetic field may depend on processing route.
The exact pathway by which microstructure and phase separation affect coercivity is not fully understood.

contradictions.description: If room temperature is intended as a processing condition, it conflicts with an intervention performed during solidification, which requires the alloy to be at or above its solidification-temperature range. The hypothesis does not clarify that room temperature instead refers only to coercivity measurement.
An annealed solid alloy cannot directly receive an intervention during solidification without being remelted; no remelting step is specified.
